source.title: Feature Integration Spaces: Joint Training Reveals Dual Encoding in Neural Network Representations

page_placements.theme: Residual magnitudes and components are predictable

record.file_problem: Minor extraction and formatting artifacts; otherwise the full text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests related claims about SAE residual structure and behavioral error using NFM residual prediction and joint training, rather than the original study's measurements of error predictability and scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper's own NFM residual-prediction and KL-divergence measurements bear on the claim. It does not measure per-token error-norm scaling or whether different SAE sizes fail on the same tokens. Claims attributed to Gurnee and other cited work are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: Only one result tests a version directly. The study replicates Gurnee's KL test on a 50k TopK SAE (OpenLLaMA-3B, layer 16): SAE splicing gives 2.99x the KL of an epsilon-random error of the same size. That bears on V3. Its other results compare its own NFM add-ons with the SAE. The NFM residual predictor takes SAE features as input, not the input activation, so it does not measure V1's linear map.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that SAE errors are pathological because the SAE misses structure in how features are integrated, not because of random noise or capacity limits. They propose that representations encode both feature identity and feature integration. Joint SAE+NFM training cuts reconstruction error by 41.3% and KL error by 51.6%, and produces a bimodal split of feature norms. Integration features have nonlinear behavioural interaction effects in 2x2 clamping experiments.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sequential NFM residual prediction and a jointly trained SAE+NFM architecture, with reconstruction and KL-divergence evaluations; it does not reproduce the original study's error-prediction and per-token scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different KL-divergence reductions for sequential versus joint training (29.8% and 51.9%, respectively); these results use different architectures and reported measurement counts.

fits_no_version.finding: An NFM fed the SAE's own features predicts part of the SAE residual. This gives a 23.4% validation error reduction, 95.5% of it from the linear term.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE residuals are partly predictable from the SAE's own latent activations, mostly linearly.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a linear+nonlinear NFM pathway lowers the KL ratio from 2.99x to 2.1x (sequential training). Training the SAE and NFM jointly cuts reconstruction error by 41.3% and KL error by ~51.9% relative to a plain SAE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding feature-interaction decoders to an SAE reduces both its reconstruction error and the pathological KL gap.

record.problems: The experiments use one 3B model, and the paper itself describes scale constraints and difficulty interpreting integration features. The joint architecture changes several components together, so the results do not identify which training choices account for the improvement.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results left out.

untested.parts: No linear regression from the input activation to the SAE error. The NFM uses SAE features as inputs.
All of it: per-token error-norm prediction, multiple SAE sizes, shared failure contexts, scaling.

There is no split of the error into a linearly predictable part and a nonlinear part, and no test of which part further dictionary learning reduces. The authors only speculate that the linear NFM gains are learnable by larger SAEs.
No circuit or steering analysis with versus without the error term.
No variation of sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents, or objective, and no end-to-end SAE. The joint model is an SAE plus a dense decoder, not a better-trained SAE.

missing.what: Control: a secondary SAE trained directly on the original SAE residuals reportedly gave no significant reconstruction gain. No numbers are given. This bears loosely on whether the error resists further dictionary learning.
Sequential-architecture KL component breakdown: linear 29.8% (t=806.3), nonlinear 0.9% (t=1375.8).
missing.locator: Results, Sequential Architecture KL Divergence Analysis

missing.what: Cross-entropy improvements of the joint model: linear 25.7%, nonlinear 4.2%, combined 26.2%.

record.verdict_notes: One model, one layer, one SAE. The record's V1 and V6 links are removed. r1 does not measure a map from the input activation, and r4-r7 compare the study's own architecture with the SAE baseline. The authors' reading (dark matter as model structure) also runs against V6's artifact framing. The NFM experiments restricted the SAE to its top 250 active features; whether the KL test used this setting is unclear. Relation stays 'tests' only on the strength of the V3 replication in r2.

versions.untested_parts: It reports how much NFM correction comes from a linear component, but does not directly measure a linear map from the input activation vector to the SAE error vector.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts across sizes, and whether errors vanish with scale.
The direct random-error comparison is reported for the sequential SAE test, not for the joint architecture.
It does not directly test whether the linear component consists of features not yet learned by the SAE or whether the nonlinear component resists further dictionary learning.
It does not measure losses in circuits, steering, or other analyses built on SAE features when an error term is omitted.

It tests whether a joint-training architecture reduces reconstruction and KL errors, but does not isolate the effects of sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents, or objective choice, nor establish that training artifacts explain most of the dark matter.
